cues.text: A Consecrated Life

According to her traditional Acts, Agatha was born to a wealthy and noble Christian family in Sicily, and from an early age consecrated her virginity entirely to God, refusing all thought of marriage.
Her beauty and evident piety drew wide attention in a Sicily still largely pagan and increasingly hostile to the young Christian faith.
Quintianus's Pursuit

A Roman official of high rank named Quintianus , aware both of her beauty and her family's wealth, pursued Agatha with repeated proposals of marriage, hoping the match would bring her fortune under his control.
When she steadfastly refused, aware that the persecution of Emperor Decius (250–253) gave him legal cover, Quintianus had her formally denounced as a Christian and brought before his own tribunal.
Trial and Torture
Tradition records that Quintianus first placed Agatha in the custody of a woman charged with wearing down her resolve through flattery, luxury, and pressure, all of which she withstood.

Failing to break her will this way, Quintianus subjected her to severe torture, including, according to her traditional Acts, the mutilation of her breasts — the detail behind her enduring iconography and her patronage of those suffering from breast disease.
Comfort in Prison
Left to die of her wounds in prison, Agatha is said in tradition to have received a vision of St. Peter the Apostle , who comforted her and healed her injuries through prayer.

Rather than release her, her tormentors returned her to further cruelty, and she died in her cell still professing her faith, still refusing to renounce Christ for the safety Quintianus had repeatedly offered in exchange for her compliance.
Ancient and Widespread Veneration
Devotion to Agatha spread with remarkable speed and reach for a local Sicilian martyr.
Her name appears in the fifth-century Martyrologium Hieronymianum and the Carthaginian martyrology of the same era.
She is praised in a sixth-century poem by Venantius Fortunatus alongside other celebrated virgin-martyrs.
By the early sixth century Pope Symmachus had already dedicated a basilica to her in Rome itself.
She is one of only seven women, besides Our Lady , named individually in the Roman Canon of the Mass.
Patroness Against Fire

Sicilian tradition credits Agatha's intercession with halting a catastrophic eruption of Mount Etna the year after her death, when citizens of Catania carried a relic of her veil in procession before the advancing lava, which is said to have stopped.
This association has made her, ever since, a patroness invoked against fire, earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions across the region surrounding Etna and far beyond.
Legacy
Agatha remains one of the most venerated virgin martyrs of the early Church, and her feast is still celebrated with enormous public devotion in Catania each February.
Her example is held up, alongside that of Sts. Agnes and Lucy, as an enduring witness to the value the early Church placed on consecrated purity, even at the cost of unspeakable suffering.
